t.altan els@49.8,95.0:
Sand dunes are the last thing you expect to find at the edge of a great freshwater-looking lake in the mountains of Mongolia, but the Uvs Nuur basin is a place of surprises. Altan Els, the Golden Sands, is a belt of dunes and sandy steppe on the shore of Uvs Nuur, the largest lake in Mongolia by area, a shallow, salty inland sea that sits in a closed basin between the Altai and the Tannu-Ola ranges, and shares its watershed with the Russian republic of Tuva. The whole basin, in two countries, was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2003 as one of the best examples of Central Asian steppe, desert and mountain ecosystems.

The variety packed into a small area is remarkable. In the space of a day's travel you can pass from snowy peaks and glaciers to larch forest, from open steppe to salt marsh and from dunes to wetlands. The lake is a huge staging post for migrating birds, with cranes, swans, pelicans and geese, and snow leopards, argali sheep and ibex live in the mountains above. Mongolian gazelles and wolves move across the steppe, and the dunes themselves shelter small mammals and reptiles. Tsugeer Els, another dune field in the same basin, and Aryskannyg in Tuva, belong to the same listing.

For riders, this is serious country, and the nearest big town is Ulaangom, the capital of Uvs province, on the south side of the lake. Paved roads are limited, and most of the way you ride on tracks of sand, gravel and hard-packed earth that can turn to mud after rain. Distances are long and navigation can be tricky, so a GPS and a paper map are both sensible, as is a bike light enough to pick up when it falls. Fuel is available only in the larger settlements, so carry extra, and plan your range carefully. Weather is changeable, with strong winds, sudden storms and cold nights even in summer. Winters are fiercely cold.

The best season is June to August, when the grass is green and the days are long, but mosquitoes can be a trial near the lake. Local herders are generous hosts, and if you stop at a ger you may be offered salty milk tea and dried curd. Greet the family, accept food with your right hand, and ask permission before taking photographs.
t.reykjavik@64.1,-21.9:
Reykjavik is the sort of capital that you could walk across in an afternoon, and that is part of the charm. It sits on a windswept peninsula in the southwest of Iceland, with painted corrugated-iron houses, the great concrete spire of the Hallgrímskirkja church, and a harbour backed by the long snowy ridge of Esja across the bay. About two thirds of Icelanders live in this region, so by Icelandic standards it is a metropolis.

The city is also a place where geology is part of daily life. Hot water for heating comes from underground geothermal fields, so the tap water sometimes smells slightly of sulphur, and the swimming pools, heated by the same source, are the social hub of every neighbourhood. People go to the pool in all weather, and soaking in a hot tub with locals in the rain is the best way to see the city. The country was settled by Norse seafarers in the ninth century, and the first Viking settler, Ingólfr Arnarson, is said to have chosen the site after throwing his high seat pillars overboard and following where they washed up.

The Ring Road, Route 1, starts here and circles the country, and the stretch to Vík crosses the south coast, with waterfalls such as Seljalandsfoss and Skógafoss. The road is paved, usually well maintained, but wind is the great hazard: gusts can knock bikes sideways and close roads, so check the forecast and speed warnings on the road. Rain, fog and cold can arrive at any time, even in summer, and the best months are June to August, with nearly endless daylight. Winter brings ice, snow and short days.

Reykjavik has everything: fuel at stations around the city, many workshops, outdoor shops for gear, and endless cafes. Fuel stations are spaced out once you leave the capital, so fill up regularly. Try a hot dog with crispy onions from a stand near the harbour, a staple of Icelandic life, and bring waterproof layers, gloves and a spare visor.
t.selfoss@63.9,-21.0:
Selfoss lies on the Ölfusá, the biggest river in Iceland by volume, which comes down from the highlands in a wide grey-green sweep and passes right through the middle of the town. With around 6,500 people it is the largest settlement in South Iceland, a farm and service town on the Ring Road, and for riders heading east from Reykjavík it is the first place with every kind of shop, cafe and fuel station. The pin sits right in the middle of it.

There is a bit of history here, too. The old suspension bridge across the Ölfusá was built in 1891 and was the longest in Iceland for a time, and it opened up the south coast to wheeled traffic. The great chess champion Bobby Fischer, who spent his final years in Iceland, is buried in a quiet churchyard just outside town at Laugardælir. West of Selfoss, the long hump of Ingólfsfjall rises above the plain, and on a clear day you can see the volcanoes Hekla and Eyjafjallajökull on the horizon, sitting like snow-capped teapots over the lowlands.

The ride from Reykjavík is not the most dramatic part of the Ring Road, but it is memorable in its own way. The road crosses the Hellisheiði lava plateau, past steaming geothermal fields, then drops to the farmland of the south, where the road is straight, smooth and fast. Wind is the main danger: gusts can be strong enough to move a loaded bike across the lane, so grip the bars and keep a gap from lorries. Weather changes quickly, with rain and sun alternating, so carry waterproofs even in July. Speed cameras and police checks are common, and fines are heavy.

Hveragerði, twelve kilometres west, is a small town of greenhouses heated by geothermal steam, famous for growing bananas and tomatoes in a country that has few trees, and its ice cream factory is a favourite stop. Þorlákshöfn, to the south-west, is a fishing port with ferries to the Westman Islands. In Selfoss itself, there are several petrol stations, supermarkets and cafés, so stock up on food and fuel before the next stretch, where services thin out.

Plan the day around the light. In summer the sun barely sets, and you can ride late into the evening, but in autumn and winter the days are short and the road can be icy.
t.ingvellir national park@64.3,-21.0:
Þingvellir is where Iceland began to govern itself. In the year 930 chieftains from across the island met at this broad valley to found the Althing, an open-air assembly that is often called the oldest parliament in the world, and it met here for the next eight centuries. The law-speaker recited the laws from a rock on the cliff, and the crowd listened from the plain below. In 1944 the republic of Iceland was proclaimed here, and the valley remains a place of national feeling.

The landscape is as dramatic as the history. Þingvellir lies in a rift valley, where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates are pulling apart by a couple of centimetres a year. The cliffs of Almannagjá mark the western edge, and walking through the gorge, you can feel the scale of it. A small waterfall, Öxarárfoss, drops into the rift, and the lake nearby, Þingvallavatn, is the largest natural lake in Iceland, clear and cold, with some of the best diving in the world in the Silfra fissure.

The ride from Reykjavik is about forty-five kilometres, and the roads are well surfaced, winding over lava fields and through low birch scrub. Mosfellsbær, about thirty-four kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, and Hveragerði is slightly closer on the other side, so top up your fuel before you arrive. The unsurfaced mountain road north from here is open only in summer, and conditions can be rough.

Weather is changeable. A sunny morning can turn into a cold, wet afternoon, so bring layers. Summer brings long light and crowds, and autumn brings colour and quiet. In winter, ice and snow can close roads. There is a visitor centre with a café and information about the geology and history. Wander the old assembly ground in the evening light and you will understand why the Icelanders chose it.
t.budir@64.8,-23.4:
Budir is barely a place at all, a handful of buildings on the south coast of the Snaefellsnes peninsula, but it has one of the most photographed churches in Iceland. The little black wooden church, Budakirkja, stands alone on the edge of a lava field with the glacier far behind, and its tarred walls and white-framed windows look dramatic against the green moss and grey sky. The present building dates from the nineteenth century and was restored in the 1980s, and it has served the surrounding farms for generations.

The lava field itself, Budahraun, is a rough, moss-covered flow with twisted rock formations, hidden crevices and a thick carpet of lichen that glows green after rain. A path leads from the church toward the sea, where a pale beach and a small crater, Budaklettur, rise above the coast. In clear weather you can see the Snaefellsjokull glacier to the west and the mountains across the bay to the south. Birdlife is plentiful, with arctic terns, eider ducks and waders nesting on the shore in summer, so tread carefully in nesting season.

The road here, Route 54, follows the peninsula's southern shore, with generous curves, good tarmac and spectacular views of mountains and sea. The traffic is light apart from tour buses, and the wind is the main hazard. In rain or fog the visibility drops and the road can feel exposed, so keep your speed measured. In summer evenings, the light on the lava field is extraordinary, and photographers often wait for the right moment.

There is a hotel nearby that has been a stopping place for travellers for many years, and an old legend says that the area was the home of Bardur Snaefellsas, a half-troll, half-human figure who is said to watch over the peninsula. The nearest village of any size is Olafsvik, about seventeen kilometres to the west, so plan your fuel accordingly.

Stop for a while, walk down to the beach and listen to the surf and the birds. It is a place where the main thing to do is simply look.
t.arnarstapi@64.8,-23.6:
Arnarstapi is a tiny fishing village on the south side of the Snaefellsnes peninsula, and the best thing about it is the coast. Basalt cliffs rise from the sea in stacks, arches and hexagonal columns, and thousands of kittiwakes and fulmars nest on the ledges, wheeling and shrieking above the surf. A footpath runs along the top between Arnarstapi and the neighbouring settlement of Hellnar, about two and a half kilometres long, and it is one of the best short walks in west Iceland.

The cliffs are the work of old lava flows and fierce Atlantic storms, and the most famous feature is Gatklettur, a rock arch that the waves have cut right through. Near the harbour you will see a large stone statue of Bardur Snaefellsas, a legendary figure with a troll's strength and a human heart, who was said to have settled the peninsula and who still protects it. The small harbour has a few fishing boats, and in summer there are a couple of places for coffee and soup.

Riding here is wonderful when the weather behaves. Route 574 loops around the western tip of the peninsula, mostly on tarmac, passing lava fields, beaches and old fishing stations. Some stretches are gravel, particularly near the more remote beaches, so be prepared for loose surface and potholes. The wind is relentless, and showers sweep in off the sea in minutes, so pack a waterproof layer and keep your speed in check on the exposed bends.

Everything here sits within the Snaefellsjokull National Park, and the glacier can often be seen towering over the village on a clear day. Arctic terns defend their nests aggressively along the path in early summer, and they will dive at your helmet if you stray too close, so stay on the marked route. Seals are sometimes seen in the bay.

Fuel is not available in the village. The nearest larger settlements are Olafsvik and Hellissandur to the north, and they are the sensible places to fill up before you set off around the peninsula. Arnarstapi is a place to stand on the cliff edge, feel the spray and watch the birds, not to rush through.
t.snaefellsjokull@64.8,-23.8:
Snaefellsjokull is a glacier-capped volcano at the western tip of the Snaefellsnes peninsula, rising to 1,446 metres above the sea. On a clear day you can see it from Reykjavik, across the bay, a white dome floating above the horizon, and it is easily the most striking sight on the peninsula. Jules Verne chose it as the entrance for his Journey to the Centre of the Earth, which has helped to cement its fame, and many Icelanders believe the mountain has a special energy.

The volcano is still considered active, although it has not erupted for a very long time, and the ice cap is shrinking steadily. Around its base lies a landscape of black lava, moss, ash and craters, protected inside the Snaefellsjokull National Park. Route 574, which circles the western end of the peninsula, gives you the best access, and the views of the glacier change with every bend.

Along the coast to the south-west you can visit Djupalonssandur, a black pebble beach among jagged lava formations, where four lifting stones of different weights were used by fishermen to test their strength before being hired for a boat. The rusted remains of a trawler that was wrecked in the 1940s still lie scattered on the shore. Nearby, the tall rock pillars of Londrangar rise from the sea cliffs, the remains of volcanic plugs, and are home to colonies of seabirds.

The riding here is memorable. The road is mostly paved and well maintained, with open curves, long sight lines and quiet stretches, though some parts are rough and gravelly. The weather can change quickly, with cloud often hiding the summit and strong wind gusting from the sea. There is a mountain track toward the glacier itself, but it is a proper off-road route that needs a suitable bike and local knowledge, so I would leave it unless you are experienced.

Bring layers, because the temperature drops sharply with the wind, and enjoy the extraordinary scenery.
t.kirkjufell@64.9,-23.3:
Kirkjufell, which means Church Mountain, is a steep, isolated peak of about 460 metres beside the sea on the north coast of the Snaefellsnes peninsula, and it is probably the most photographed mountain in Iceland. It rises close to the little fishing town of Grundarfjordur, with a smooth, pointed outline that looks something like a witch's hat or an arrowhead, depending on the angle. You may recognise it from television, where it appeared as a mountain in a famous fantasy series.

The best view is from the small waterfall called Kirkjufellsfoss, just across the road, where the stream tumbles in a series of little cascades with the mountain framed behind it. Photographers come here from all over the world, especially in the evenings and during the northern lights season, so the car park can be busy. In summer the sun hangs low for hours, creating long, golden light on the rock, while in autumn and winter the green aurora ripples across the sky above it.

The riding to get here is a pleasure. Route 54 follows the northern shore of the peninsula past dark beaches, small harbours and wide bays, with the sea on one side and jagged mountains on the other. The surface is mostly good, with long straight stretches, and the traffic is usually light. Wind and rain are the main hazards, and the mountains can disappear in cloud within minutes, so be patient and wait for the weather to clear.

The mountain itself was formed by glaciers during the ice age, which carved away the softer layers of rock and left the harder core standing alone. It is possible to climb it, but the path is steep and exposed, and has been the scene of accidents, so it should be treated with real respect.

Fuel is available in Grundarfjordur, a few kilometres away, and in Olafsvik, and there are cafes and a small museum in the town. This makes a good finish to a day on the peninsula, with the mountain glowing in the late evening sun.
t.krabi@8.1,98.9:
Krabi is the sort of place that makes visitors reach for superlatives and then settle for pointing. Limestone karst rises straight out of the mangrove and the sea, with sheer grey cliffs wrapped in jungle and topped with pinnacles, and the town sits on the Krabi river as it widens into a muddy estuary. Out in the bay, long-tail boats run to the islands and the beaches around Ao Nang, which has turned into a lively resort strip about twelve kilometres west. The town itself, with about thirty thousand people, has a riverfront promenade and a busy night market where the day's catch ends up on the grill.

Riding out of Krabi on a bike is a pleasure, though not for corners. The roads are mostly good tarmac, with a few long straights between oil-palm plantations and rubber trees, and then sudden short climbs where the road cuts around the karst. The heat and humidity are constant, and in the rainy season, from May to October, downpours arrive fast and turn the road slippery. Dry season, from November to April, is the better window, with cooler mornings and clearer views.

Thai traffic takes some getting used to. Motorbikes outnumber cars, overtaking happens on both sides, and dogs wander across the road without much concern. Keep your speed modest, look well ahead at junctions, and wear a helmet, because police do check and it is the law. Fuel is easy to find on the main roads and in town, usually at stations with a small shop selling cold drinks and snacks.

Food is the highlight. Southern Thai cooking is spicier than the central version, with plenty of coconut milk, turmeric, and fresh seafood grilled over charcoal, and the night markets serve it at prices that make hotel breakfasts look silly. Try a bowl of curry with rice noodles for breakfast like the locals, then fill up on fresh fruit. The day's ride from here heads north and east across the peninsula, through rubber country and low hills, toward Nakhon Si Thammarat.
t.ingvellir@64.3,-21.1:
In the year 930, Icelandic chieftains gathered on a grassy plain beside a rift valley and founded a parliament, the Althing, and they kept meeting here for nearly nine hundred years. Þingvellir, the Parliament Plains, is the place where a nation made its own laws in the open air, standing beside a rock called the Law Rock, and the site is now a national park and UNESCO World Heritage site. The words of the law speaker, reciting the code from memory, carried across the plain.

The setting is as extraordinary as the history. Þingvellir lies in a rift valley where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates are slowly pulling apart, about two centimeters a year, and you can walk down a long gorge, Almannagjá, between the cliffs of the western plate and the floor of the valley. Beyond lies Þingvallavatn, the largest natural lake in Iceland, clear and cold, and Silfra, a fissure of astonishingly clear water that divers swim through. Birch scrub and moss-covered lava fields fill the valley, with a small white church and farmhouse beside the river.

Þingvellir is also the first stop on the Golden Circle, the standard tourist loop that runs to Geysir and Gullfoss waterfall. The road from Reykjavik, about forty-five minutes away, crosses a heath of lava and moss, with gently rolling curves, and it can be busy with tour buses and rental cars in summer. The surface is good, but the weather is the issue: wind can be fierce, and rain, fog and sudden gusts can make riding unpleasant. Gravel on road edges and sheep on the road are other hazards.

Summers are cool and bright, with nearly endless daylight in June, and the best months are June to August. In winter, ice and snow close the road at times, and the auroras may show. Dress warmly in layers whatever the season, because the wind off the lake can cut through even a summer day.
t.thingvellir@64.3,-21.1:
Þingvellir is the place where Iceland began as a country, and it is one of the few spots in the world where history and geology tell the same story. In the year 930, chieftains from across the island met on a plain beside a lake to set up the Alþingi, an assembly that is often described as the oldest parliament in the world still in some form existing. They gathered each summer at the foot of a great rock wall, listened to the Lawspeaker recite the law from memory, settled disputes and sometimes executed offenders in the river. Around the year 1000 the assembly decided that Iceland would adopt Christianity, and in 1944 the republic was proclaimed here.

The landscape is the second half of the story. Þingvellir sits in a rift valley where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates are slowly pulling apart, and you can see the break in the cliffs of Almannagjá, a long fissure that frames the walk down towards the plain. Behind it is Þingvallavatn, the largest natural lake in Iceland, with water so clear that divers come to swim in the fissure called Silfra. The area is a national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with birch scrub, lava fields and a quiet river called Öxará that falls into the rift as a small waterfall.

The riding is easy and quite pretty. From Reykjavík side the road climbs gently over the moorland and then drops toward the lake, in long, open bends on good tarmac. Beyond the park, the road to Laugarvatn and the Golden Circle passes through lava fields and wide valleys. In summer it is very busy with coaches and rental cars, so early morning or evening are better, and the speeds are low, with police and cameras in evidence. Wind can be fierce on the open plain.

There is a visitor centre with a cafe, and car park charges apply at the main sites. Mosfellsbær, the nearest large town on the Reykjavík side, has plenty, and Selfoss and the small town of Laugarvatn are good further along the circle. Fill the tank before you get here.

Take half an hour to walk the path along the fissure. The wind, the lake and the grass-covered ruins of old booths give you a sense of what it meant to gather here. Dress warmly, because even in summer the weather can turn quickly.
t.geysir@64.3,-20.3:
The word geyser comes from this place. Geysir, the original, sits in the Haukadalur valley in the south of Iceland, in a patch of steaming, bubbling ground that has been famous for centuries. The great Geysir itself has been mostly dormant for long periods, waking now and then after earthquakes, but its neighbour Strokkur more than makes up for it. Every few minutes the water in the pool domes up, turns a glassy blue and bursts into the air, typically ten to twenty metres high, before collapsing back with a rush. The crowd that has gathered, phones raised, lets out a collective gasp every single time.

The area is a geothermal field, with hot springs, mud pools and vents steaming in the cold air, and the ground is coloured with yellow sulphur and orange mineral crusts. The smell of sulphur hangs over everything. Paths and ropes keep visitors away from the scalding water, and it is important to respect them, because the water can be near boiling and the ground edges can be fragile. Do not touch the water, and keep children close.

The ride into the valley is on Route 35 through the open farmland and low hills of the south, an easy road with long straights, gentle bends and big views of the mountains and, on a clear day, the glaciers of the interior. Traffic is heavy in summer, with tour buses on a fixed schedule and rental cars driven by people who are not used to Icelandic roads, so patience matters. Crosswinds can be strong on exposed sections. Early mornings and evenings are quieter and the light is lovely.

Across the road from the geothermal area is a large complex with shops, a restaurant and a cafe, so food and warm drinks are easy. It is the kind of place where you can get a bowl of soup and a hot chocolate, then buy a woollen hat you did not know you needed. For fuel, you should not count on it here, and the safer plan is to fill in Selfoss, Flúðir or Laugarvatn along the circle.

Gullfoss, the great two-stage waterfall of the Hvítá river, is only a short ride beyond, and the pair together make the heart of the Golden Circle. Watch Strokkur from the upwind side if you want to avoid a drenching, and check the forecast before you go, because it is not a place you want to be in freezing rain.
t.kerid@64.0,-20.9:
Kerið is a volcanic crater with a lake in the bottom, and it is one of those places that looks as though someone staged it. The walls are a deep rusty red, made of scoria, the porous volcanic rock that forms when lava cools quickly, with patches of moss and grass clinging to the slopes. In the middle is a pool of intensely blue-green water, which shows up especially well against the red on a bright day. The crater is about two hundred and seventy metres across and the lake is shallow in places but deep in others.

It sits along the Grímsnes area in south Iceland, a short ride from Selfoss, and it is one of the easiest stops of the Golden Circle. There is a small car park, and an entry fee is usually charged because the land is privately owned. A path runs around the rim and another leads down to the water's edge, and you can walk around the whole circuit in a short time. In summer, birds nest in the crater and the air carries the smell of wet moss and cold stone, while in winter the lake freezes and the red slopes are dusted with snow.

The riding on this section is gentle. The roads are paved, the bends are broad, and the landscape of farms, greenhouses and low hills is soft compared with the more dramatic parts of the country. This region is warmed by geothermal heat and many of the greenhouses grow tomatoes and cucumbers in the middle of an Icelandic winter. Keep an eye on speed, as police patrols are common near tourist sites, and watch for sheep and slow-moving farm vehicles.

Wind is a factor at any time of year and it can be strong on the exposed rim, so hold on to your hat and keep your gloves on. A rain jacket is a good idea even on a bright morning.

Fuel and food are straightforward. Selfoss, thirteen kilometres away, is a proper town with pumps, a big supermarket and plenty of cafes, and Hveragerði, a little further, is the greenhouse town known for its hot-spring baths and bakeries. If you are doing the whole Golden Circle in a day, filling in Selfoss before or after Kerið is the natural rhythm.

The crater was long thought to be the result of a collapsed volcanic cone, a magma chamber that emptied and fell in on itself. Whatever the exact history, it makes for a very satisfying ten-minute stop on a longer day of riding.
t.borgarnes@64.5,-21.9:
Borgarnes sits on a narrow peninsula pushing out into a wide, shallow fjord, and when the tide is out, the water turns into a shining flat of sand and mud with birds feeding in it. The town is small, about 1,800 people, and it is the main settlement of the Borgarfjordur district in west Iceland. It is a natural stopping point on the way north from Reykjavik, and most people use it for a quick coffee or fuel before heading on, which is a pity, because there is a good story here.

The story is Egil's Saga, one of the great Icelandic sagas, which follows the poet and warrior Egill Skallagrimsson, whose father Skalla-Grimur settled this land in the ninth or tenth century. Egill was a fighter, a farmer and a poet of unusual gifts, and the saga is full of feuds and sharp-tongued verses. The Settlement Centre in town tells the story of the settlement and the saga in an engaging way, and there is a statue of Skalla-Grimur's nurse, Brakar-Ey, on the small island nearby, who the saga says was killed while saving him.

The drive here from Reykjavik is easy, passing under the Hvalfjordur fjord through a tunnel of nearly six kilometres, free of tolls since 2018, and then across low, wind-blown country. Weather is the main hazard: in winter, ice and strong crosswinds can close roads, and even in summer a headwind can eat your fuel. From Borgarnes you can turn west onto the road to the Snaefellsnes peninsula, which is the subject of this ride, with its lava fields, black beaches and the glacier-topped volcano at the end.

Fuel is available in town, and the stations are open long hours in summer. There are several places to eat, including a restaurant with a view over the fjord, and a supermarket if you need to stock up before the peninsula, where shops are fewer. A short walk along the shore at low tide is worth the time. Late June to August offers the best weather and the longest daylight.
t.gullfoss@64.3,-20.1:
Gullfoss, the golden falls, is the great set piece of the Golden Circle, the tourist route that links Þingvellir, Geysir and the waterfall in a long day out of Reykjavík. The river Hvítá, fed by the glacier Langjökull, comes sliding down a gentle slope and then drops in two stages, first a broad step of about eleven metres and then, at right angles, a plunge of twenty-one metres into a narrow, twisting canyon. The spray rises in a cloud, and in sunshine there is almost always a rainbow over it.

There is a story attached to the falls that Icelanders tell with pride. In the early twentieth century, foreign investors wanted to use the river to make electricity, and the owner of the land, a farmer, leased it to them. His daughter, Sigríður Tómasdóttir, is remembered as the woman who campaigned against the scheme, walking to Reykjavík to find a lawyer, and the deal eventually collapsed. Today the falls are protected, and a small memorial stands near the path.

You can walk right to the edge of the upper fall, along a path that is slippery with spray, or look down from the platform above. The canyon below is cut into basalt, and the water inside it is a boiling, roaring grey, an impressive sight. In summer the car park is crowded with coaches, and in winter the path can be icy, with the falls draped in ice, so wear good boots. The best time to visit is early in the morning or late in the evening, when the crowds are fewer and the light is softer.

The riding on the Golden Circle is easy, on good tarmac, with long views across lava fields and pastures, but the wind can be fierce, especially on the open stretches, and rain can arrive in minutes. Pumps are mostly unmanned, and need a card with a PIN, so keep it handy.
t.geysir area@64.3,-20.3:
The word geyser comes from this place. The Great Geysir, in the Haukadalur valley in southwest Iceland, gave its name to every spouting hot spring in the world, though it has become mostly dormant, erupting only rarely after earthquakes. The whole area is a geothermal playground. The ground is stained yellow, orange and white by minerals, steam rises from vents, and pools of turquoise water bubble gently within circles of rock. Behind the field, a slope covered in grass and low shrubs rises to a ridge with a view down across the valley and the plains beyond. Fuel is not available at the site itself, and the nearest town of any size is Selfoss, a good thirty kilometres or more away, so fill up on the way. The nearby waterfall of Gullfoss is only a short ride along the same road, and the two make a natural pair.

Stand upwind of Strokkur, because the spray and sulphur smell can drift over you. Watch the blue bulge swell before the eruption, and you will have time to raise your camera before it blows.
t.laugarvatn food@64.2,-20.7:
Laugarvatn is a small settlement on the shore of a lake of the same name, and the name tells the story: laug means hot spring and vatn means water. The lake is fed partly by geothermal springs, so the shore is warm in places, and steam rises from the ground around the edge. The village itself is modest, a school, a few guesthouses, a café or two and a spa where visitors sit in steam rooms and warm pools beside the lake, but its position midway between the Geysir area and Þingvellir makes it one of the natural stopping points on the Golden Circle.

The local speciality is rye bread baked in the ground. Bakers bury pots of dough in the hot sand by the lake and leave them for a day, and the bread comes out dark, dense and slightly sweet. It is served with butter and sometimes with smoked trout, and you can taste it in the café and at demonstrations by the shore. It is a simple, odd and delicious example of how Icelanders use the heat under their feet, and it is a good reason to stop for food.

The riding to Laugarvatn is easy and scenic. Route 37 and the roads around it run through lava fields covered with moss, over low ridges and past farms, with the shape of the Hekla volcano visible to the south on clear days. The surface is paved and generally good, with gravel on side roads. The weather is changeable, and a sunny start can turn to rain by midday, so carry waterproof gear. Wind off the lake can be bracing, and in summer the evening light is long and golden, with a pale sky that never quite darkens.

To the west lies Þingvellir, where the Icelandic parliament, the Althing, first met in 930, making it one of the oldest parliamentary assemblies in the world. The site sits in a rift valley where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates are pulling apart, and you can walk through the gap between them. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the landscape is as dramatic as the history.

Fuel is available at Laugarvatn, but it is worth checking hours and keeping the tank topped up, because the nearest larger towns, Selfoss and Hveragerði, are over thirty kilometres away. Pumps often take cards only. Bring a swimsuit if you want the spa, and a dry layer for afterwards.
t.reykjavik@64.2,-21.9:
Reykjavík is a small capital of about a hundred and twenty thousand people that behaves like a bigger one. The city sits on a windy peninsula in the south-west, with the sea on three sides and a ring of mountains across the bay, and it is heated almost entirely by geothermal water, piped in from the ground. The outdoor swimming pools, filled with hot water, are the social centre of the city, and a morning soak with the neighbours is part of local life. The landmarks are the concrete tower of Hallgrímskirkja, whose design echoes the basalt columns of Iceland, and the glass facade of the Harpa concert hall by the harbour.

For a rider, Iceland is a country of extremes, and the weather is the first of them. The summer riding season runs from June to August, when the light is nearly endless and the roads are open, but wind and rain can arrive at any time, with gusts strong enough to move a loaded bike. Dress in waterproof layers, check the forecast daily and pay attention to the road warnings. The Ring Road, Route 1, is paved, but there are gravel sections elsewhere, and the high-country F-roads are for four-wheel-drive vehicles only.

The long day heads south-east along Route 1 to the coast, past the waterfalls of Seljalandsfoss and Skógafoss, to the harbour at Landeyjahöfn, where a ferry crosses to the Westman Islands. Surtsey, the youngest island in the world, rose from the sea in a volcanic eruption that began in 1963, and is now a protected research site. Landing is not allowed, so you see it from the sea or the air, and the ferry is the nearest approach. The coast road has long, straight stretches with the glacier Eyjafjallajökull in view.

Fuel is easy in the capital and along Route 1, but stations are widely spaced in the empty parts, so fill up when you can. Food is not cheap, though a hot dog from the famous harbour stand is an institution, and so are lamb soup and fresh fish. Watch your speed, since fines are high, and take a bath in a hot spring if you can. The long summer evenings make the drive a pleasure.
t.hella@63.8,-20.4:
Hella is a small town in southern Iceland, on the banks of the Ytri-Rangá river, about a hundred kilometres east of Reykjavik on Route 1, and it is the place where most riders go to get ready for the interior. Its population is a few hundred, but it serves a wide farming district of horse studs, sheep, barley fields and greenhouses heated by geothermal water. Looming to the north-east, on a clear day, is Hekla, the volcano that medieval Europeans called the gateway to hell. It rises to nearly 1,500 metres, has erupted many times, and last did so in 2000, when it gave only a few hours of warning.

The river here is famous for salmon, and a few caves carved by hand into the soft sandstone nearby are some of the oldest human-made structures in Iceland, probably dug by Irish monks or early settlers, though no one is sure. To the west, the Þjórsá, at some 230 kilometres the longest river in the country, runs down from the highlands in a broad, grey torrent. The land is flat and green, with the occasional black lava rock showing through, and the horses graze beside the road.

For a rider, Hella is the start of the Sprengisandur road, one of the great highland tracks of Iceland, which crosses the interior between the Hofsjökull and Vatnajökull glaciers to the north. The route is classed as an F-road, which means it is rough, unbridged in places and open only for a short season, usually from late June to September, depending on snow. Rivers must be forded, the surface is volcanic gravel and sand, and it is no place for a road bike. A heavy adventure machine with experienced riders and good planning can do it, but weather and river levels decide the day. Check conditions with the road administration before leaving.

Fuel is available in Hella, and the sensible thing is to fill the tank and carry extra, because there is none at all in the interior. Selfoss, about thirty kilometres west, is the larger town for supplies and repairs. Buy food and water here, and eat well in the café before you go. The wind can be strong, so keep a firm grip, and enjoy the smell of wet grass and sheep as you leave the farms behind.
t.golden circle point 2@64.3,-21.1:
Þingvellir is the one place in Iceland where geology and history are inseparable. The national park sits in a rift valley, a wide, grassy trough bounded by cliffs, where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates are slowly pulling apart. You can walk between the walls of the fissure and feel the gap, and in the lake beside it divers swim between continents.

In 930 the Icelandic chieftains gathered here for the first time to form the Althing, one of the oldest parliamentary institutions in the world, and for the next nine centuries the assembly met on the plain each summer. Laws were recited from the Lögberg, the Law Rock, and disputes were settled, feuds were stopped or started, and people from all over the island camped in turf booths. In 1000 the Althing voted to adopt Christianity, a decision that shaped the country. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and for Icelanders it is a place of deep national feeling.

The riding approach is pleasant, with the road climbing from the coastal plain and then descending to the lake of Þingvallavatn, the largest natural lake in the country. The bends are gentle and the surface good, but the traffic can be heavy in summer, and the car parks fill up. Early morning is the best time, when the light is low and the crowds not yet there.

Nature is full of detail. The lake is fed by cold clear springs, and the water is so clear that visibility under the surface is extraordinary. Birch scrub and moss-covered lava cover the ground, and the Öxará river drops into the rift at the waterfall of Öxarárfoss. Birds nest in the cliffs, and the smell of damp moss and cold water is strong.

Services near the park are limited to a visitor centre and basic facilities, so Reykjavík and the town of Selfoss are the main centres for supplies. Wind off the lake is strong, so dress for a chill even in July.
t.golden circle point 3@64.3,-20.3:
Geysir is the word that gave the world its geysers, and the original is still here, in the Haukadalur valley, a basin of steaming ground, blue pools and mineral-stained earth. The Great Geysir itself has been mostly dormant for many years, with only occasional activity, but its neighbour Strokkur obliges the crowds every few minutes, throwing a column of water high into the air with a deep gurgle and a sigh.

Approaching the area is straightforward. The road crosses open farmland and gentle hills with the distant glaciers of Langjökull and Hekla on the horizon, and the surface is generally smooth with moderate traffic. The park is a short walk from the parking, and the ground is hot and fragile, so stay on the paths. The smell of sulphur is unmistakable and the steam drifts across the road on cold days, which can be briefly confusing at speed.

The geology behind it is simple but spectacular. Water seeps deep into the volcanic rock, is heated by magma, and is forced back to the surface in explosive bursts. The mineral deposits form colourful crusts around the pools, and the hot springs make the surrounding ground steam in winter. The name comes from the Old Norse verb to gush, and the site has been described by travellers since the Middle Ages, and travellers have been describing it for centuries.

Nature around the area includes geothermal vegetation, with algae and mosses that thrive in the warm water, and in the surrounding countryside, Icelandic horses graze on the fields. Many visitors enjoy a break at the visitor centre across the road, which has food, shops and a decent cafe, and which is among the better-served stops on the Golden Circle.

Timing matters. Mid-morning to mid-afternoon the crowds are heaviest, and early or late is better for photographs. Be careful of wet ground and sudden spray, and of heavy gusts on the open plain.
t.golden circle point 4@64.3,-20.1:
Gullfoss is the waterfall that sums up Iceland: a huge volume of glacial water from the Hvítá river dropping in two steps into a narrow canyon, with spray hanging in the air and rainbows appearing on sunny days. The upper fall is wide and the lower one plunges into a crevice at right angles, so the water seems to vanish into the earth, and the noise is a constant, low roar that you feel in your chest.

The ride here is easy and pleasant. The road crosses open upland, with the Langjökull glacier on the horizon and the river winding through the valley, and the bends are gentle. The surface is generally good, but wind and rain can come in suddenly, and in winter ice and snow close or restrict the road. The car park is a short walk from the falls, and the paths can be wet and slippery from the spray.

The falls were once threatened with a hydroelectric scheme, and local legend says that Sigríður Tómasdóttir, the daughter of the farmer who owned the land, walked to Reykjavík and threatened to throw herself into the water if the plan went ahead. The details of the story are partly folklore, but the falls were eventually protected. It is a nice tale about how a country decided what it valued.

The nature around the falls is bleak and beautiful. Low scrub, moss and grasses cover the plain, and the canyon walls are streaked with mineral colours. The mist from the falls supports a surprising amount of life, and in summer the air smells of wet stone and fresh water. The glacier river brings milky grey water from the ice cap to the north.

From here the Kjölur highland road heads north into the interior, a gravel route for those with the right bike and the right season. Services at the falls include a visitor centre with food and shops, so you can usually get a hot meal. Go in the morning, when the sun lights the spray, and wear warm and waterproof clothing.
t.snaefellsnes peninsula loop point 2@64.8:
Búðir is one of those places that looks like it was designed by a film director. A small black wooden church stands alone on a green headland, with a vast lava field spreading behind it, the sea ahead and, on a clear day, the white dome of Snæfellsjökull glowing in the distance. There is no village to speak of, only a hotel, a few scattered farms and the church, and it is the sort of scene that makes you reach for the camera before you have turned off the engine.

The lava field around Búðir, called Búðahraun, was formed by an eruption several thousand years ago, and it is now covered in moss, lichen and low scrub, with the sharp, folded forms of the lava forming small caves and gullies. A short walk from the church takes you down to a golden beach, one of the few on the peninsula, where the sand is light and the surf rolls in from the open Atlantic. Eider ducks and arctic terns nest nearby in summer.

The road along the south coast of Snæfellsnes is well maintained and a pleasure to ride, with long open bends, big skies and views across Faxaflói to the distant mountains of the mainland. The surface is good, but the wind off the sea can be strong, and rain squalls move in quickly. Traffic is light outside the high season, and there is little here to disturb the peace.

The church is of historical interest as well as beauty. A church has stood here for centuries, serving a trading post that once flourished at Búðir, a place where merchants from Europe bought dried fish and wool from the peninsula's farmers. The black tar that protects the wood is traditional, and the church is a popular place for weddings, which is easy to understand.

Services are minimal, with a hotel and restaurant on the spot, and the towns of the peninsula, such as Ólafsvík, are some distance away. Come in the evening, when the low sun lights the lava and the church, and the day's visitors have gone.
t.snaefellsnes peninsula loop point 5@64.9:
There is a mountain on the north coast of Snæfellsnes that has become one of the most photographed in Iceland, and it is easy to see why. Kirkjufell, the church mountain, rises sharply from the shore near the town of Grundarfjörður, a steep, pointed cone of rock that looks like a hat put down in the wrong place. In front of it, a small stream tumbles down in a series of falls, and the combination of mountain and water has been in more films and photographs than anyone can count.

The ride along the north coast is spectacular. The road follows the shore of the Breiðafjörður, with views across the bay to the mountains of the Westfjords on a clear day, and the bends are open and gentle. The surface is generally good, with some patchy sections after winter. In summer there is traffic, as the mountain is a favourite stopping place, and the car park fills quickly. Early morning or evening is better.

Kirkjufell is about 460 metres high, made of layers of lava and sediment, and it is a demanding scramble for walkers, with several accidents on the steep upper slopes, so keep to the lower paths unless you are experienced. The mountain was given a new fame when it appeared as the arrowhead mountain in a popular television series, which brought a wave of visitors.

Nature around the mountain is rich. The shores of the fjord are good for seabirds, including eider ducks, and in some seasons whales are seen from the coast. The grass is green and the air smells of sea and wet earth. In winter, the northern lights appear above the peak, and photographers come from across the world.

Grundarfjörður is a small fishing town with services, including shops and cafes, and it is the practical place to stop. Ólafsvík and Stykkishólmur lie on either side. Try to arrive when the light is low, and expect the weather to change.
t.kjolur highland road point 1@64.3,-20.1:
The Kjölur road begins at a waterfall, which seems about right. Gullfoss, on the Hvítá river, marks the end of the busy Golden Circle and the start of a track into the empty middle of Iceland, a road called the Kjölur, or keel, because it runs like the ridge of a boat between two great glaciers. Behind you lie coach parks and cafes. Ahead, after the last farm, there is nothing but moorland, lava and sky.

The highland road is a different kind of riding. It is a gravel F-road, not paved, with corrugations that rattle fillings, loose stones in the corners and long straight stretches where the wind blows from every direction at once. It is open only in the summer, typically from some time in June until September, depending on snow, and conditions change from week to week, so check the road authority's information before you set out. This is a road for a bike and a rider who are ready for gravel, not for a loaded tourer on road tyres.

The country it crosses has a history of its own. For centuries this was a route across the interior for travellers going between the north and south of the country, used by farmers, outlaws and people fleeing the law. Stories of ghosts and trolls are told about the lava fields, and the old cairns that mark the way are still there beside the track. In the nineteenth century, a few brave travellers began to cross it for pleasure, and the modern road was only built in the twentieth century.

The landscape is stark and beautiful. To the west is the flat white dome of Langjökull, Iceland's second largest glacier, and to the east lies Hofsjökull. Between them the plateau is a mix of black sand, moss and scree, with the occasional blue lake. The air is thin and cold, with a mineral smell.

There are no towns on the track, so bring what you need and tell someone where you are going. The nearest facilities lie at the falls behind you, and in the summer at a highland hut ahead. Take it slowly, and enjoy the quiet.
t.sprengisandur highland road point 1@63.8:
Hella is a small town on the Ytri-Rangá river, in the south Icelandic lowlands, and for riders heading into the interior it is the last place that feels like ordinary rural life. The land here is flat and green, with farms, horses and the occasional lava outcrop, and on the horizon the great snow-covered cone of Hekla, one of Iceland's most active volcanoes, rises above the plain. The mountain is a constant presence, and it has been erupting, on and off, for centuries.

The ride from here toward the Sprengisandur highland road begins gently, along the lowlands, and then climbs onto the moors. The landscape changes quickly, with the farms thinning out and the grass giving way to sand and lava. The roads on the highland routes are gravel, mostly unpaved, with river crossings in places, so this is a ride for a bike set up for the job and for riders who have checked conditions. Weather can change quickly, and rain and wind come with little warning.

The district has a long history. Not far to the east lies the area that features in Njáls saga, the most famous of the Icelandic sagas, in which a tale of feud and revenge unfolded in the lowlands, ending in a famous burning. Hekla itself was believed in the Middle Ages to be the gateway to hell, and the legends of the mountain were widely known across Europe. Today farmers keep sheep and horses in the shadow of the volcano, and a well-organised rural economy hums along.

Nature is varied. The lowland meadows are rich in birds, with golden plovers and whimbrels, and the rivers hold salmon and trout. Ash from many eruptions has built up in the soil, and on a clear day the whole landscape has a sharp, fresh feel.

As a small town, Hella has shops, a service station and basic services, and is the sensible place to prepare for the interior. Selfoss is larger, some thirty kilometres to the west. Pack warm clothing and check the highland road conditions before you set out.
